cited_evidence.text: In 2014, the first superconducting high-entropy alloy Ta0.34Nb0.33Hf0.08Zr0.14Ti0.11 (in at.%) was discovered []. According to Sun and Cava [], this alloy can be classified as a type-A HEA superconductor. HEAs of this type contain only metals on the left side of the transition metal region of the periodic table, crystallize in a body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice, and exhibit superconducting transition temperatures (Tc) between 4.0 and 9.2 K, while their highest upper critical field (μ0Hc2) is close to 12 T [,,,,,,]. These are the most widely studied HEA superconductors to date. However, it should be noted that most of these alloys contain a large amount of niobium and tantalum, while the titanium concentration is typically less than 20 at.%. Because binary Nb-Ti alloys exhibit much better superconducting properties than Nb-Ta [], it is plausible to expect that NbTi-based high-entropy alloys will have a higher Tc and/or μ0Hc2 compared to previously reported type-A HEA superconductors. Moreover, in the case of various ternary Nb-Ti-Hf and Nb-Ti-Ta and quaternary Nb-Ti-Ta-Hf alloys, the highest values of μ0Hc2 were observed for the titanium-rich alloys []. The superconductivity of disordered materials has been extensively studied because of an observation made on the insulator-superconductor transition or disorder-induced superconductivity. In addition, recent studies on BiS2-based layered superconductors have shown the importance of controlling the local structural disorder to improve superconducting properties. As a new category of disordered superconductors, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are alloys containing five or more elements with an atomic concentration between 5 and 35%,, have been extensively studied, leading to the discovery of a wide range of HEA superconductors. One of the notable features is the difference in characteristics of superconductivity among conventional metal or alloy superconductors, superconducting thin films, and HEA superconductors,. decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has focused on their mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and superconductivity. Recent studies have explored the effects of different elements on the properties of these alloys, including the role of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr in refractory high-entropy alloys. The discovery of superconductivity in a uranium-containing high-entropy alloy has expanded the class of materials to include actinide elements. However, the understanding of superconductivity in high-entropy alloys is still limited, and further research is needed to establish the mechanisms governing superconducting behavior in these materials.
decision.unsolved: The mechanisms governing superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys, particularly in uncharacterized high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes, are not well understood. The effects of different elements on superconductivity in these alloys are still being explored, and the relationship between the composition and superconducting properties of high-entropy alloys is not yet fully established.
decision.why: A systematic variation of composition would allow researchers to establish the relationship between the composition and superconducting properties of high-entropy alloys, and to identify the key elements and mechanisms governing superconducting behavior in these materials.
